title: Portfolio CMS
description: A custom local content management system that generates the fully static React portfolio you are viewing.
longDescription:
Portfolio CMS is a bespoke local content management system designed to streamline personal website updates without the overhead of a traditional database or paid hosting platform. The primary goal is to provide a rich visual editing environment on a local machine that ultimately outputs a fully static, single-page HTML file. What sets this architecture apart from standard platforms is its zero-runtime philosophy and self-referential nature: the very website you are currently browsing was generated by this software. Instead of relying on a live backend or fetching data from an API, the CMS injects all text and media data directly into the React site template as an embedded JSON block. This approach eliminates server costs, removes database maintenance, and guarantees instantaneous load times for the end user.

The authoring workflow operates entirely through a lightweight Node and Express server running locally. Users manage content via a custom vanilla JavaScript admin panel, which features a drag-and-drop interface for ordering projects and integrating YouTube previews. When media is uploaded, an automated processing pipeline takes over. It converts legacy image formats to optimized WebP files, applies necessary EXIF rotation fixes, and automatically routes the assets into category-specific folders. Once the content is ready, the user triggers a publish script that merges the local JSON data files with the front-end template, generating a single, self-contained HTML file that can be pushed directly to GitHub Pages.

The underlying technical engine balances a robust local backend with an exceptionally lean production frontend. The local server utilizes Express for routing and file management, paired with Sharp for high-performance image processing. The administrative interface is styled with Tailwind CSS and uses Quill for rich text formatting. For the live site, React 18 and Babel run directly from a CDN, parsing the embedded JSON payload upon loading. This complete decoupling of the authoring environment from the public-facing deployment results in a highly secure, maintainable, and cost-effective personal portfolio system.
specs:
Framework: React 18 (CDN), Node.js

Language: Vanilla JavaScript

Backend: Express, Sharp, Multer

Styling: Tailwind CSS, Quill

Storage: Local JSON (filesystem)

Deploy: GitHub Pages (static output)

title: Immersive Dance Lighting Rig
description: Temple Nightclub | San Francisco - The main room remodel at Temple San Francisco wraps a 208V curved video ceiling and 10 custom pixel pillars into a flat-black, switched-relay infrastructure built across a two-year pandemic shutdown.
longDescription:
The main room at Temple Nightclub in San Francisco required a dense hybrid lighting, pixel and video rig that could vanish entirely into the dark when unlit. I designed the system around a curved video ceiling wrapping behind the DJ, 10 custom LED pixel pillars, beams, wash's, profiles, all built in flat black. Before aesthetic integration could even start, the physical ceiling forced a massive life-safety detour. Because the curved video wall blocked standard fire suppression coverage, I brought in a fire crew to reroute the sprinklers both above and below the solid ceiling plane using side sprayers with a 15 ft reach. When we found the main sewer drain blocked, we had to run the drainage above grade through an alley test valve and cut in a new low-point basement drain just to clear the system.

Powering that density without burning equipment lifespan meant overhauling the venue's electrical capacity with new 400A and 200A services. I split the load across two new panels: 24 circuits of 208V on twist-lock connectors dedicated exclusively to the video ceiling, and 60 circuits of standard 120V Edison for the lighting. Rather than relying on independent wall switches, I wired the entire rig onto switched relays grouped in clusters of 4. That setup gave us centralized shutdown so fixtures would not sit sucking dust and burning hours during dark days, while hardwired house lights let staff handle maintenance without booting the show systems.

What was supposed to be a three-month build turned into a two-year pandemic ordeal where I cycled through three separate crews and stepped up to manage electricians, plumbers, and carpenters directly. The hardest recurring fight was not mechanical, but restraint. The owner and creative director wanted every fixture and screen blasted at 100% all the time. I argued that crowding that many lights into a small room is about having angles and combinations, like a single-color sweep or white eggbeater prisms, not raw brightness. When we finally opened and they tested that full-blast look on the crowd, the patrons rejected it within 10 minutes. When we ran the rig my way, linking the Resolume and Madrix engines across the ceiling, pillars, and scrap-built VIP tape walls, the entire room lit up on the first try without a single glitch.

title: Emmy Stand
description: I built a desktop display stand to house and illuminate a friend’s Emmy without melting the PLA+ enclosure.
longDescription:
An old coworker from my Tracks days won an Emmy and asked for a custom display. We used to work together when he was a bartender, so he knew my lighting background. I built him a desktop rig that scaled ballet lighting principles into a PLA+ enclosure.

The stand runs 512 addressable WS2815 LEDs across 7 data lines, driven by a Wasatch Pixels Basic Eight controller hidden inside the base. There are 3 boom towers per side with frosted lenses that arch back from downstage to upstage, while 45 deg wall washers sit recessed along the outer edges. A black and white film strip lines the bottom, printed in dual materials for diffusion and masking. The curved backdrop was too large for a single Bambu Lab print, so I built it in modular sections and turned the seams into an exaggerated surface texture.

Packing 144/m density LEDs into closed plastic is basically building a slow toaster. To keep heat from destroying the display from the inside out, I locked the current limit to 3A at 12V in WLED before I powered it on for the first time. I programmed the fixture in my dark apartment. When I set the Emmy on the pedestal, the reflective gold finish mirrored the light sources more than it absorbed the illumination, creating a warped mirror effect across the metal.

LEDs: 512 (144/m)

Driver: WS2815 (RGB)

Firmware: WLED

title: LithoLab
description: A fully browser-based web application for generating custom-shaped, multi-color 3D printable lithophanes with AI-assisted design tools.
longDescription:
LithoLab is a client-side web application designed to generate high-fidelity, custom-shaped lithophanes for 3D printing. While standard generators are restricted to traditional four-color CMYK constraints, LithoLab supports customizable, multi-color palettes to achieve superior color accuracy in the final physical print. The project differentiates itself by introducing custom masking capabilities that trim the lithophane into non-standard shapes, along with generating an independently exportable geometric border for polished, multi-part assemblies.

The system architecture was developed by porting the open-source PIXEStl backend to execute entirely within the browser, avoiding server-side processing overhead. The workflow is managed through a custom frontend interface where users upload source imagery, define masking parameters, and configure border dimensions. Upon export, the software isolates the customized border as a discrete 3D object, allowing users to assign specific filaments and colors when preparing the files in slicing software like Bambu Studio.

The standout technical achievement is the robust JavaScript implementation of the modified PIXEStl engine, paired with an integrated Google Gemini API for generating base images, structural masks, and file metadata. To solve the hardware constraints of color mapping on advanced machines like the Bambu Lab X1C, a dedicated companion utility called LithoPalletGen was built in parallel. This secondary application handles precise color palette generation, import/export functionality, and material calibration to ensure accurate physical reproduction of the digital models.

gallery.caption: The LithoLab workspace links source image manipulation directly to physical 3D print parameters. In the main canvas, users apply custom geometric masks and adjust spatial orientation, while the sidebar controls physical dimensions, border scaling, and filament palette selection. The dual-preview engine at the bottom provides immediate feedback, displaying both a palette-accurate color rendering and a surface-texture depth map to verify print accuracy before exporting.

title: Unfold
description: A React based web application featuring interactive card decks designed to facilitate meaningful conversations and reconnect people.
longDescription:
Unfold is a web application designed to help users reconnect with friends and family when relationships become routine. The interactive card game provides structured questions across four distinct decks to prompt reflection and meaningful dialogue. Unlike standard physical card games, Unfold adapts to user preferences by offering three distinct play modes, including a curated journey sequence that gradually deepens the interaction. The digital format optimizes the experience for remote communication over video calls.

The development process began with rapid prototyping using the Lovable platform to establish the core user experience and interaction logic. Following the initial proof of concept, the project was migrated to a dedicated GitHub repository for independent development and architectural refinement. The primary workflow centers on user choice, allowing individuals to pull from specific decks, combine all cards randomly, or set a defined number of prompts for a structured progression. This flexible logic ensures that users can tailor the depth and pace of their conversations.

The application operates on a modern React and TypeScript foundation that prioritizes performance and data privacy. The technical core utilizes a custom state management layer built with React Hooks and the LocalStorage API, ensuring all sensitive user interactions remain securely on the client side. The front end integrates Tailwind CSS and Radix UI primitives to deliver an accessible, responsive, and visually refined interface. This UI architecture maintains fluid transitions and robust state handling during complex card drawing interactions.

title: Pixel Pyramid
description: Trapped LED heat inside a sealed, 3 material PLA+ pyramid print required software current limiting to prevent structural melting.
longDescription:
Getting crisp pixel isolation without light bleed across an internally divided pyramid required printing the entire sculpture as a single piece. Each cell needed a black core to block light from adjacent shafts, white walls to bounce illumination upward, and a frosted PLA+ shell for diffusion. Building that geometry without manual post-processing meant committing to a 1 to 3 day continuous print cycle on a Bambu Lab X1C, with 3 filament swaps on every single layer and a mountain of purge waste.

Trapped LED heat nearly killed the design during burn-in testing. I lifted the sculpture after a long run and accidentally mushed the softened grid with my thumb. Venting the back enclosure helped, but drilling holes into the frosted top shell would have ruined the display.

To keep the structure solid without sacrificing visual punch, I swapped the hardware to 12V WS2815 matrices and set a 1A current limit in WLED. Keeping the diodes over 1 cm from the surface eliminated visible hotspots while letting the grid show through the frost. The finished piece hung at Glow Lounge in Denver and ran for days at a time without warping, becoming the foundation for a fabrication process I still use.

title: Pixel Mini Pyramid
description: An 8x8 pixel matrix desk lamp powered over 5V USB-C with a scannable QR code base.
longDescription:
Stepping down from my 16x16 matrix to an 8x8 desk piece meant solving a packaging problem. I modeled the Pixel Mini Pyramid in SolidWorks and Blender around an ESP32 running WLED on 5V USB-C power. The base doubles as a scannable QR code that links to my site.

Squeezing 64 LEDs into the small footprint left very little room for hardware. The USB-C port wanted to push back into the case whenever I plugged a cable in, and closing the shell kept crushing the internal wiring. It took several 3D printed iterations and test fits to anchor the controller securely and route the leads cleanly.

A short throw distance usually creates hotspots. I used a frosted diffusion layer over white cell walls to break up the light, and printed the case in 3 materials on an X1C. A few friends and family have them on their desks now, and the QR code base still scans on the first try.

title: Pixel Plane Warp
description: By combining black light-isolation walls with reflective white cell linings and frosted diffusion, this sweeping surface installation achieves sharp, vibrant patterns at low operating temperatures and current limits.
longDescription:
I destroyed an early print trying to push enough light into the high corner of the wave. The piece is a subdivided grid with a sweeping surface distortion that terminates in sharp points. Because the peak sits far above the LEDs, lighting the far corners required running the strips at full brightness. The trapped heat ruined the print. Plastic and hot LEDs do not get along.

I modeled the unit in SolidWorks for dimensional accuracy. A Bambu Lab X1C printed the unified model with black walls to isolate each light channel. For the final version, I lined the cells in white and added a frosted layer. That combination let me cap the WLED output on the ATHOM ESP8266 controller to a 1A limit at 12V without losing clarity.

It ended up on the ceiling at Glow Lounge for a while. In a dark room, the black walls disappear and leave only the distorted pattern floating overhead. The simple geometry did the work without needing to fight for brightness.

title: Field Solder Station
description: A portable, field soldering station designed to streamline complex live entertainment installations.
longDescription:
The field solder station is a highly compact, tool carrier engineered to solve the logistical challenges of on site LED installations. Working in unconventional locations like high ladders or cramped spaces under a stage requires immediate access to tools without the burden of a bulky bench setup. This solution differentiates itself by consolidating an entire soldering toolkit into a single portable chassis driven by a standard USB PD battery bank.

This tool emerged from an iterative prototyping process tested directly in the field during a major San Francisco nightclub installation. Initial concepts explored integrated batteries and complex wiring before the design converged on a simplified approach to maximize reliability and reduce weight. The final iteration logically organizes a TS100 or TS101 iron, solder spool, a bottle of flux, desoldering pump, wick, wet and wire sponges, and rubber feet into an optimized spatial layout.

I designed the chassis in SolidWorks to tightly pack the required tools into a minimal footprint. Fabricated from PLA using Bambu Lab 3D printers, the structure leverages precision tolerances to secure mechanical hardware like the dual helping hands through a robust friction fit. This precise 3D modeling eliminated the need for secondary mechanical fasteners, resulting in a streamlined and self contained system that reliably supports mobile fabrication work.

title: LED Pixel Panel
description: Temple Nightclub | San Francisco - A high-impact LED ceiling installation engineered for ultra-low headroom environments using custom-modified dancefloor PCBs.
longDescription:
The objective was to create an immersive LED pixel lighting design for the basement level of Temple nightclub in San Francisco despite severe headroom limitations. This project diverges from standard fixture installations by utilizing custom-modified LED dancefloor PCBs repurposed for ceiling mounting. By stripping the technology down to its bare circuit boards, the design achieves a massive visual impact within a fraction of the traditional spatial footprint.


The workflow began by sourcing an LED dancefloor manufacturer and collaborating directly with them to engineer custom boards. The physical design required specific functional alterations, including adjusted pixel spacing, enlarged mounting holes, 90-degree wire headers, and a specialized protective backing material. For the physical integration, an aluminum T-track system was mounted directly to the ceiling infrastructure, allowing the custom PCBs to bolt securely into the track for a seamless fit.


The primary engineering achievement was compressing a high-density lighting matrix into a total vertical profile of under one inch. The system operates on a 24-volt power architecture and utilizes WS2818 addressable pixels. The selection of WS2818 components ensures robust performance through redundant data transmission, preventing single-pixel failures from interrupting the visual array during demanding live operations.

title: LVL
description: Temple Nightclub | Denver - An electrical and data overhaul of an immersive pixel lighting rig to ensure stability and enable 3D voxel mapping.
longDescription:
The LVL room at Temple Denver features an immersive, exclusively pixel-based lighting installation with continuous lines running across the floor, ceiling, and pillars. The core goal of this project was to execute a comprehensive structural rewiring of the power and data distribution to transform an unstable installation into a robust, production-ready system. Unlike standard rig assemblies, this overhaul required retrofitting an existing design, demanding precise power management and signal integrity to support advanced, whole-room spatial mapping without compromising the original aesthetic.

The project workflow centered on meticulous hardware restoration and systemic reconfiguration. Every segment of the existing LED tape was systematically removed, rigorously tested, resoldered, heat-shrinked, and reinstalled to guarantee structural and electrical integrity. To handle the data load, the LED decoder lines were strategically decentralized across the network. Concurrently, the entire power infrastructure was redesigned, efficiently routing power from supplies located in the back room and beneath the DJ booth to ensure consistent performance across the venue's footprint.

The primary technical constraint of the installation was the extreme length of the pixel runs, which inherently caused severe voltage drop and data signal degradation. This was overcome by running DC wire in parallel with the LED strips to introduce strategic power injection points, guaranteeing uniform brightness and absolute data stability. With the hardware stabilized, the entire room was 3D voxel mapped, allowing the control system to execute volumetric, full-room effects like spatial line sweeps. By isolating specific structural elements into distinct groups, the system can also effectively simulate the behavior of traditional lighting fixtures within a continuous pixel environment.

title: MIRUS
description: Mirus Art Gallery | Denver - I wired an RGBW wash lighting system into hanging wooden baffles 12 ft above MIRUS Art Gallery.
longDescription:
On my first install for the company, someone else handed me a parts list and told me to build a ceiling rig at MIRUS Art Gallery in Denver. Another contracting team had already hung the wooden louvers 12 ft in the air. That meant I spent the project on a scissor lift, adhering RGBW strips into routed channels overhead. If I had chosen the materials, I would have spec'd addressable pixels for full mapping across the room. Instead, I worked with wash strips driven by Madrix Basic, keeping the entire room on 1 DMX universe.

The routed channels in the baffles ended in 90 degree corners. Forcing the LED tape around those sharp turns snapped the copper backing on my first attempt. Because they were wash strips instead of pixels, the repair was simple. I cut out the broken module at each corner and soldered jumper wires across the gap to the next copper pads.

Up in the 6 ft plenum above the ceiling, I stashed the high current supplies and DMX decoders. Each supply group controlled 16 baffles. The spec'd power units were thin and ran with loud fans, which usually spells trouble in an art space. Luckily, the gallery connected to a club room with a Funktion-One sound system, so ambient noise swallowed the fan hum.

Because the gallery walls are painted white, the saturated colors transform the space. Flip the rig from white illumination to psychedelic chases, and the whole room changes. The client loved it.

title: Inflatable Tubes
description: Reelworks | Denver - To get eight inflatable tubes to cut through a club lighting rig, you cannot use off-the-shelf LED tape.
longDescription:
The centerpiece for Track's Denver Pride 2023 was a forest of eight custom inflatable tubes rigged to the ceiling beams with wire cable. To get the brightness I needed, I had custom 24V redundant-data pixel module strands made with double-sided clear lenses, then ran two 30m or 23m strands in parallel inside each tube, securing them directly to the internal fabric ties. Because running that much LED load over a single line would cause massive voltage drop, I put a power supply at both ends of every tube and severed the positive wire at the midpoint to prevent the units from back-feeding into each other. I fed and tested the guts on the floor, hoisted the tubes empty, and powered the fans and decoders once they were in the air.

During load-in and testing, the Resolume Arena control system and wireless decoders worked without a hitch. The problem started when 2,000 people walked into the room with cellphones in their pockets. The saturated RF environment completely choked the wireless signal. Data rates dropped to roughly 5fps, and the tubes repeatedly lost connection and defaulted. Luckily, I had programmed their default state to a static Pride palette, so when the signal dropped, the centerpiece stayed on theme.

The inflatables ran warm, but the double-stranded clear-lens build pushed out enough light and resolution that another local fabricator called me after the show to ask what hardware I was using. I got them through the weekend on the fallback palette, and told the venue to replace the wireless units with hardwired decoders before the next run.

title: GeoLens Pro
description: GeoLens Pro is a local-first PWA that automatically sorts and annotates field photos using GPS geofencing.
longDescription:
GeoLens Pro is a mobile-first Progressive Web Application designed to help field professionals capture, organize, and annotate site photos without manual filing. The primary goal is to eliminate the tedious, error-prone process of sorting hundreds of images after site visits. Unlike standard photo galleries or cloud-dependent CRMs, this application leverages a localized GPS auto-sort engine. By establishing geofenced boundaries around specific job sites, the app automatically routes incoming photos into the correct project folder the exact moment they are captured.

The workflow centers around a localized architecture that requires no account creation or backend synchronization. Users define job locations on an interactive map and set a custom geofence radius. When a photo is captured via the live camera integration or imported from the device, the system extracts the GPS coordinates and calculates the distance to all active job origins. If the photo falls within a defined radius, it is instantly assigned to that job. Users can then open the integrated canvas editor to apply non-destructive annotations, modify layers, and export professional PDF reports directly from the browser.

The standout technical achievement is the real-time client-side sorting engine powered by the Haversine formula and Dexie for IndexedDB storage. Built with React and TypeScript, the application handles complex geographical calculations and persistent data management entirely within the browser environment. Leaflet manages the interactive map boundaries, while exifr handles metadata extraction for imported files. The custom canvas editor supports granular per-layer transformations and interfaces directly with jsPDF to generate structured inspection reports without relying on a remote server.

title: PixelForge AI
description: An interactive generative artwork studio that uses controlled text hallucinations to kickstart creative visual exploration.
longDescription:
PixelForge is an interactive web application designed to kickstart creative exploration by bridging abstract text generation with high-fidelity image synthesis. Unlike conventional generation interfaces that rely strictly on literal user inputs, PixelForge utilizes controlled AI hallucinations to construct poetic, open-ended prompt foundations. This approach pushes image models past predictable outputs and gives creators a sandbox to discover nuanced visual concepts through either category-focused or open-ended random generation.

The system workflow coordinates a multi-stage creative pipeline. Activating the randomizer triggers targeted prompt frameworks that generate abstract, poem-like descriptions. Users maintain full creative control with the ability to inspect, refine, or manually edit these text outputs prior to rendering the final image. As generations occur, the platform automatically maintains a comprehensive session history on the left sidebar. This allows users to compare iterative variations, review parameter metadata, and package assets into bulk ZIP downloads directly within the workspace.

Built on React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS, the application integrates the Gemini API for prompt generation and the Imagen API for visual rendering. A primary technical hurdle involved overcoming model output convergence, where similar prompts yielded overly repetitive visual styles. To solve this, the application features a manual model selector within the settings menu. This allows users to route identical prompts across different model versions to leverage their distinct stylistic interpretations. Local data persistence relies on IndexedDB and LocalStorage to manage client-side image storage and history tracking without external database dependencies.

title: Chronicle: Iterative Fiction Engine
description: Chronicle is a zero-build, browser-based interactive fiction engine that generates multimodal, AI-driven storytelling in real time.
longDescription:
Chronicle is a browser-based interactive fiction engine designed to dynamically generate text, images, and audio for a cohesive choose-your-own-adventure experience. It shifts away from standard conversational AI interfaces by enforcing a rigid narrative structure through strict schema validation. This approach ensures every generated turn consistently delivers prose, four distinct choices, scene illustration prompts, and backend lore updates, creating a predictable game loop without relying on a traditional server.

The application operates entirely client-side using a zero-build React architecture with ES modules and Tailwind CSS. During a session, a user selects a genre and visual style, initiating a turn loop that builds a layered system prompt based on player decisions. The system manages state by maintaining a persistent memory stack, compressing older narrative beats into long-term summaries while preserving recent verbatim prose and relevant character lore. When a player makes a choice, the engine merges the updated codex, appends the new beat, and processes parallel requests for image and audio generation to construct a complete multimodal page.

The standout technical achievement is the memory engine and structured data parsing powered by the Google Gemini API. By utilizing a strict JSON response schema, the application guarantees that the large language model outputs precisely formatted game data for immediate UI rendering and state management. The engine also tackles the challenge of long-context drift in AI storytelling by filtering and injecting only the most relevant codex entries per turn. Additionally, the system supports real-time text streaming by parsing partial JSON outputs and includes resilient fallback integrations for both text-to-speech and image generation.

title: Strata - Digital Notebook
description: A serverless, browser-based note-taking application combining block-level editing with infinite canvas workspaces and Google Drive synchronization.
longDescription:
Strata is a client-side note-taking application designed to provide hierarchical organization alongside flexible visual workspaces. The primary goal is to deliver a robust productivity tool that runs entirely in the browser without relying on a dedicated backend server. The project differentiates itself by seamlessly blending structured, block-based text editing with an infinite drawing canvas, utilizing the user's existing Google Drive as the primary cloud storage and database mechanism.

The engineering workflow focuses on delivering a resilient user experience that bridges offline availability and cloud connectivity. The application caches data locally using localStorage for immediate access and pushes updates to Google Drive via automatic debounced saves. The project is currently an active work in progress, with current development focused on resolving known sync issues and refining conflict resolution logic. The development journey included prototyping a standalone desktop variant to enable direct webpage embedding, but active development has pivoted back to the web application to maximize accessibility and maintain a streamlined user workflow.

The core application is built with React and styled with Tailwind CSS, maintaining a strict zero-dependency architecture outside of the necessary Google APIs. A major technical component of the build is the in-browser Babel transpilation, which allows the application to function entirely on the client side. The infinite canvas relies on custom coordinate system handling with viewport culling and real-time SVG path rendering to ensure smooth panning, zooming, and drawing performance. By directly integrating with the Google Drive API, the system can bypass traditional server storage limitations while natively embedding Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides directly into the workspace.

title: IdeaForge.AI
description: IdeaForge.AI is a comprehensive ideation pipeline that transforms raw thoughts into actionable project strategies utilizing a serverless Google Drive backend.
longDescription:
IdeaForge.AI is a multi-stage idea sifter designed to capture, expand, and execute concepts without initial critique. The core goal is to provide a frictionless environment where users can verbally or textually dump ideas and seamlessly transition them into fully realized projects. This application differentiates itself by completely eliminating traditional cloud database dependencies, opting instead to use the user's personal Google Drive and Google Sheets as the sole backend architecture.

The workflow begins with an uninhibited idea dump, where users log their thoughts to be automatically tagged and summarized. When an idea shows promise, it is promoted to the brainstorm phase where an AI assistant conducts an interview to extract deeper details and compiles a structured breakdown. Promoting the brainstorm to a project generates an execution strategy, an expense tracker, and a task list. Finally, the campaign section conducts a comprehensive interview to compile a playbook, breaking down discovery, monetization, distribution, and logistics into actionable phases.

The application frontend is built with React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, utilizing Vite for optimized builds. The standout technical achievement is the custom data layer that interfaces directly with the Google Sheets API and Google Drive API, transforming a standard spreadsheet into a fully functional database. A local database implementation handles offline state and data reconciliation, while a user-provided Gemini API key securely powers the core intelligence for summarizing concepts and generating execution playbooks.

title: CharGen.AI
description: CharGen.AI is a comprehensive, client-side character development engine utilizing Google AI for text and image generation.
longDescription:
CharGen.AI is a universal character development engine designed to build highly detailed profiles for any archetype, ranging from humans to complex sci-fi and fantasy subjects. The primary goal is to provide a unified workspace for character creation that seamlessly bridges the gap between statistical attributes and visual representation. Unlike standard text-based character generators, this platform features a unique bidirectional workflow. Users can define over 100 conditional attributes to synthesize distinct reference images, or they can reverse the process by using vision models to extract structured physical and psychological data directly from an uploaded piece of reference art.

The application operates entirely on the client side to prioritize user privacy and eliminate traditional backend infrastructure. Users navigate through an eight-section attribute builder that dynamically adapts its input fields based on the selected species type. As users modify attributes, generate custom outfits, or draft backstories, all data is saved persistently in the browser using IndexedDB. When a user initiates a generation request, the application bundles the current character state and interfaces directly with Google API endpoints. The state management system coordinates these external responses, updating the local character library in real time and allowing users to organize, bulk export, or iterate on their designs without a central server.

The platform is engineered using React 18 and Vite, relying on Zustand for efficient state management across the complex, deeply nested attribute trees. The standout technical achievement is the synchronized integration of Google Gemini 2.5 Flash for nuanced text generation and image analysis, alongside Imagen 4.0 for high-fidelity visual synthesis. By committing to a strictly serverless architecture, the system requires users to supply their own API keys, guaranteeing zero telemetry and eliminating hosting costs for heavy AI workloads. This constraint necessitated the heavy optimization of IndexedDB to reliably store and manage large payloads of image data and complex JSON character objects locally within the browser.

title: LithoPalletGen
description: A vanilla JavaScript color calibration tool utilizing area-averaged pixel sampling for precise multi-material lithophane generation.
longDescription:
LithoPalletGen is a specialized color calibration application designed to streamline multi-material lithophane workflows by accurately mapping printed filament swatches. Unlike standard single-pixel color pickers, this tool utilizes a configurable area-averaging eyedropper that samples regions ranging from 32 to 256 pixels. This distinct approach neutralizes surface noise, lighting variances, and filament translucency, ensuring statistically accurate color profiles that reflect the physical characteristics of the printed material.

The tool operates through a split-pane interface that directly pairs a canvas-based image viewer with a hierarchical palette builder. Users upload photographs of physical prints and systematically construct multi-layer color profiles, categorizing base colors alongside ordered layers of increasing material thickness. As users sample the image, a live-updating bounding box overlays the canvas, aggregating color data across hundreds of pixels to actively filter out the textural inconsistencies inherent in FDM prints.

Engineered as a zero-dependency vanilla JavaScript application with no build step, the system operates entirely client-side, utilizing IndexedDB for persistent image storage and localStorage for palette serialization. The core technical achievement is the real-time pixel averaging engine, which rapidly executes per-frame getImageData computations across large pixel arrays while maintaining fluid cursor responsiveness. A unified color model anchors the architecture, driving a dual-format export system that outputs PIXEstl-compatible JSON in either HSL or hex notation for immediate downstream processing.

title: Field Bench PSU
description: A compact, 3D printed bench power supply designed for testing LED lighting installations in the field.
longDescription:
The Field Bench PSU is a portable tool designed to power and test diverse LED products during on-site installations. While standard bench power supplies are bulky and tied to AC mains, this custom unit leverages modular components and a highly versatile interface architecture to provide reliable testing capabilities directly on the job site.

The physical enclosure was modeled in SolidWorks and fabricated using PLA+ for structural durability. The internal hardware workflow routes power from a 5521-DC input jack through a mini rocker switch into the voltage conversion module. The output side maximizes field flexibility by providing a 5525-DC jack alongside a pair of banana plug jacks equipped with wire screw terminals. This layout allows the hardware to interface with a wide array of standard connectors, or rely on bare wire connections paired with WAGO terminals for rapid setup.

The primary technical driver is an embedded buck-boost converter capable of handling a 5 to 32VDC input and delivering an equivalent voltage output at up to 5A. A standout operational achievement is the integration of standard USB PD sources, allowing the system to accept a 19V 100W input and reliably convert it to precise 5V, 12V, or 24V outputs. This capability ensures immediate, adaptable power delivery for any low voltage LED architecture encountered in the field.

title: Club Lexi
description: CrazyHorse | Denver - I packed 64 fixtures into a low-ceiling basement club using flush-mounted strut channel and DJ-proofed standalone control.
longDescription:
Club Lexi is a basement with three areas (a lounge, a bar, and a main dance floor), all trapped under a ceiling just short of 10 feet. Patrons could jump and touch the rig. Standard box truss would have eaten too much headroom, so I hung the entire system from strut channel mounted flush to the drywall. Working flush against a ceiling means you have zero room above the fixture to route cable or hide a mess. Everything is exposed. I had an electrician drop power at pre-planned locations on dedicated switches, which let the venue kill half the rig across two zones during early hours without touching the software.

I ran 64 fixtures over 4 universes on a single Wolfmix WMX1. Fitting hybrid profiles and moving heads into a room that low meant watching every inch of clearance. Because the venue operates without a lighting technician, the WMX1 sat in the booth for the DJs to run standalone.

Handing live control to DJs immediately exposed the weak points. They would twist knobs, drag fade times to a crawl, and assume the rig was broken when the lights stopped responding. They also loved to mash the strobe button until the room was unreadable, and running a Radiance Hazer from the controller turned into a mess. I locked the hazer to a low-output toggle, set up a hard reset so they couldn't trap the program in a crawl, and let the rig do what I built it to do.

title: The Orb
description: Temple Nightclub | Denver - An 8 foot diameter kinetic LED sphere featuring complex voxel mapping and remote high current DC power distribution.
longDescription:
The Orb is an 8 foot diameter kinetic lighting centerpiece designed for Temple nightclub in Denver. The primary objective was to deliver a massive, three dimensional visual experience that physically interacts with the crowd by moving dynamically on a motorized hoist during headliner performances. It stands apart from standard LED installations by intentionally maximizing negative space within the aluminum frame to create a true volumetric 3D effect rather than a solid luminous surface.

Inheriting the project in an unfinished state required an immediate evaluation of the system architecture to ensure structural safety and electrical reliability. The physical build involved securing hundreds of individual LED pixel modules to the frame while carefully managing weight and visual sightlines. To preserve the open aesthetic, only the data decoders were housed inside the sphere. The bulky power supply units were relocated above the ceiling, requiring thick gauge copper wiring to transport the power safely down the hoist lines and into the moving structure.

The core technical achievement of this build was engineering safe and reliable high current DC power distribution over a significant distance. Mitigating the voltage drop from the remote ceiling power supplies to the suspended orb required precise load calculations and rigorous power protection methods. On the control side, the physical layout of the LEDs was translated into an exact 3D voxel map using Madrix software to enable complex volumetric lighting programming.

title: The Basement
description: Triangle Bar | Denver - I bounced upward pixels off ceiling slats to light a 10 ft basement club in Denver.
longDescription:
The basement at Triangle in Denver had a concrete ceiling under 10 ft high. I handled the entire build solo as an independent contractor, covering design, procurement, installation, programming, and training. Hanging moving lights overhead meant rotary-hammering 8 pieces of strut channel directly into the ceiling with 2 to 3 anchor points per piece. Working alone on a ladder, the hardest part was simply holding a fixture in place with one hand while threading a bolt or seating a cable with the other.

I despise looking directly at bare sources. Instead of covering the overhead array in standard diffusion, I pointed the pixel modules upward to bounce light off the ceiling slats. The reflected light bled through the gaps, creating a smooth gradient overhead without blinding the crowd. I also isolated the power supplies in an adjacent room to keep fan noise out of the club. I did not know fanless supplies existed at the time, but the quiet room made programming and maintenance much easier.

To bridge the gap from the remote racks to the ceiling array, I used long-range decoders. The run distance was short enough for standard decoders, but I wanted to test the hardware on a live build. During testing, loose connections at 2 points caused the ground to drop and the pixels to flicker. Because pixel runs work cleanly up to a break, finding the fault points was straightforward.

The indirect wash turned a hidden basement into an intimate club. Venue owners and patrons loved the clean look, and hiding the rig in the ceiling structure kept the low room from feeling crowded.

title: Vertical Pixel Bar Tubes
image: media/Lighting/Vertical Pixel Tubes - Que Bueno Suerte!/20240619_122306.webp
description: Que Bueno Suerte! | Denver - Restoration of a custom, high-channel-count LED installation integrating recycled fluorescent tubes into a modernized venue network.
longDescription:
This project involved the structural restoration and system integration of a legacy lighting centerpiece suspended above the main bar at Que Bueno Suerte!. The primary goal was to salvage an inherited visual asset constructed from recycled four-foot and eight-foot fluorescent tubes and bring it online with a newly installed venue-wide control system. The key differentiator was the strict constraint of working within a pre-existing physical framework, which required reverse-engineering and modernizing a failing, custom-built design rather than executing a standard blank-slate installation.

The physical workflow required systematically uninstalling dead fixtures, separating the three-tube clusters, and extracting the degraded LED tape from the core of each bundle. Concurrently, the electrical infrastructure underwent a complete overhaul to replace obsolete decoders housed in custom overhead power boxes. This hardware intervention established the necessary communication link, bridging the repaired legacy physical structures with the modern, centralized data network governing the rest of the venue's lighting.

The upgraded fixtures utilize 5V WS2813 LED strips, selected specifically for their backup data line to provide signal redundancy and prevent future cascade failures within hard-to-access overhead locations. Because the physical design dictated maintaining the original 60-pixel-per-meter density, the resulting display requires an astronomical channel count to operate. Managing this immense data footprint required integrating upgraded decoders capable of processing high-density pixel output while staying continuously synchronized with the venue's overarching control system.

title: Pixel Negative "X"
description: An internal X obstruction inside each cell turns a white square into an array of 1024 converging arrows.
longDescription:
I wanted to build the pixel diffusion equivalent of a stage gobo. I designed an X obstruction through the center of 256 isolated cells in SolidWorks. Powered off, the piece sat like a plain square. Powered on, the solid X blocked the center of each WS2815 LED and created 4 arrows pointing toward each other.

My first attempt on a Tenlog TL-D3 failed when the nozzle dragged across the X pattern and caused layer shifts. Printing directly against the buildplate kept the face flat. A 1 mm PLA+ face provided the right balance of diffusion and opacity without bleeding light between cells.

I capped the current in WLED on an ATHOM ESP8266 controller to stop the PLA+ from heating and warping. Running fluid patterns across the grid made the uniform obstructions look fuzzy and ripply.

title: Pixel Seed of Life
description: A 1mm face printed over a subdivided matrix hides the seed of life until the pixels fire.
longDescription:
I built this as a proof of concept to expand what I could do with subdivided matrices. Printed face down, the piece looks like a white square when turned off. Getting that surface required a 1mm face. That thickness balanced structural stability and light transmission without showing bleedthrough from the black walls behind it. With a 10mm throw, bouncing the light was unnecessary.

Heat became the immediate problem. Early tests ran at full brightness inside sealed enclosures. Over time, the corners curled and the grid walls softened enough to move by hand. Without vent holes on the back, the units bowed away from the wall as the PLA+ heated up. Adding vents and limiting current in the firmware stopped the deformation.

Now the symbol stays hidden until the matrix powers on. Lighting large clusters of pixels reveals parts of the pattern across the surface. The complete shape only appears when every pixel is active.

title: Pixel Celtic Owl
description: An internally subdivided 16x16 LED matrix housed inside a dual-material relief sculpture of an organic Celtic owl.
longDescription:
My workstation laptop crashes if I calculate an internal grid larger than 16x16. This piece was a test to see if I could map that geometric matrix inside an organic shape. I bought an owl model online and split the workflow between SolidWorks and Blender for the first time. The processing load of subtracting those 256 cells from Celtic knotwork pushed my hardware to its limit.

Early attempts on a Tenlog TL-D3 IDEX printer leaked light everywhere. Stopping the bleed between cells took 0.8 mm walls of black PLA+, which meant 2 passes with a 0.4 mm nozzle. Moving the job to a Bambu Lab X1C with an AMS unit solved the bleed immediately. A 0.4 mm wall of black PLA+ now isolates every cell cleanly.

The front relief is thin enough to act like a lithophane. When powered off, it reads as a white carving in a black frame. Turn on the ATHOM ESP8266 controller, and the 16x16 grid cuts straight through the surface lines.

title: Lobby Wall
description: Tracks | Denver - I built a double-sided wall of LEDs for Tracks in 5 days after soldering 5000 joints by hand.
longDescription:
Tracks could not close for a remodel, so we had 5 days between open weekends to install a double-sided wall of LEDs and as part of a full remodel. It sits right at the entrance where people walk in. To hit that window, another tech and I spent weeks in the club basement and my home shop building modular panels off site. Each 2x4 pegboard panel held 520 raw LED pucks contact-cemented in 8 pixel configurations. Instead of buying pre-made strands, we manually soldered custom wire lengths using lamp cord for power injection, leaving us with over 5000 solder points before we ever hung a panel.

We mounted the rows of pegboard modules to the wall and wired each row to a dedicated output on a 16 output SanDevices E682 decoder running WS2801 protocol. Frosted plexiglass sheets on standoffs covered both sides to diffuse the light. I mapped the array using Madrix 3.6 software.

This was my first LED pixel build, and the initial test run was rough. The pixels flickered badly across the wall. I had not linked grounds across multiple power supplies, and I did not know about power injection yet. Adding inline resistors at the inputs smoothed out the data signal, and I later retrofitted power injection at the midpoint. The E682 is a Christmas light decoder and not very rugged, but it worked.

When we opened the doors that Thursday, regulars gasped walking into the room. Teaching myself pixel mapping on that build launched an entire lighting design focus in my career, even if I should have just bought pre-made LED strands.

title: Curved Liquor Bottle Display
description: Que Bueno Suerte! | Denver - I designed and hardwired 96 custom louvered corner fixtures to illuminate a see-through sheet metal bottle shelf without blinding guests.
longDescription:
Off-the-shelf extrusion was out of the question for the main bottle display at Que Bueno Suerte!. I wanted to aim light up at the bottles from the corners of the display sections without putting a lens or diffuser in front of the LEDs, preserving maximum throw distance and brightness. To keep raw diodes out of the guests' eyes, I 3D printed custom corner fixtures with integrated light-blocking louvers. Getting the louver spacing and angle right took a few rapid prototyping iterations, and the alignment pins snapped off on almost every print, but the LED tape track itself held the end caps in line.

The shelf is a see-through metal grid, which made hiding the wiring for 96 individual fixtures a project in itself. I handwired the entire array and wrapped the routing in black tubing secured with mini zip ties. Because there was no closed conduit to hide inside, I used double-sided foam tape to mount the louvers and leaned on the physical stiffness of the bundled wire to support its own weight across the grid.

In action, the shelf is mapped into the rest of the venue's LED pixel installations through a centralized Madrix server, running unified, building-wide dynamic looks. It worked cleanly until the restaurant opened for dancing and guests started abandoning drinks on every flat surface in the room. I had built the shelf for empty display bottles and never anticipated liquids up there. Spills dripped into the tracks and corroded the LED tape, and because of how the louver tracks were dimensioned, standard waterproof silicone tape would not fit as a drop-in replacement. I ended up requesting a sign to keep drinks off the display and keeping spare parts on hand.

title: Extrusion Centering Sled
description: A custom modular 3D printed alignment jig designed to perfectly center LED extrusion tracks on uneven nightclub pillars.
longDescription:
This project required designing a custom alignment tool to install LED strip extrusions on the foundational pillars of Temple nightclub in San Francisco. The primary goal was to achieve visually perfect vertical alignment of center tracks on boxed pillars that were irregularly shaped and wavy. Unlike standard measuring methods, this unique solution utilized a physical jig that referenced the outer edge tracks to automatically find the relative center at any given height, ensuring the final installation appeared flawlessly straight.

The workflow began with a rudimentary prototype using scrap material and a ruler to test the alignment concept. The final tool functioned as a dynamic sled that rode inside the center LED extrusion track during the physical installation. As the jig slid upward along the track, notched ends highlighted with yellow china marker allowed for constant visual verification against the outer corner extrusions. This continuous referencing system made it possible to secure the center track with a pneumatic nailer progressively, actively compensating for the hidden waves in the underlying pillar casing.

The standout technical achievement was engineering a rigid tool that bypassed spatial manufacturing constraints. Because the required length of the jig exceeded the available 3D printer build plate, the component was designed as a four-part modular assembly. These interlocking sections maintained the structural integrity required to withstand the physical forces of the pneumatic nailing process while keeping the sled firmly on track. This custom hardware solution successfully transformed a highly irregular architectural environment into a precise, uniform lighting canvas.

title: Dance Floor Pillars
description: Temple Nightclub | San Francisco - A ruggedized 320-meter pixel mapping installation engineered to deliver floor-to-ceiling architectural lighting within an immersive nightclub environment.
longDescription:
The Temple Nightclub San Francisco main room remodel required powering and controlling 320 meters of high-density pixel tape across ten floor-to-ceiling architectural pillars. The primary objective was to immerse the dance floor in dynamic lighting while protecting fragile electronics from direct crowd contact. Unlike conventional stage lighting that operates at a safe distance, this installation integrated custom illumination directly into public structural elements, requiring a tamper-proof and visually seamless enclosure system that extends from the dance floor to above the main high-resolution LED video ceiling.

To achieve a clean aesthetic and prevent physical damage from venue patrons, the structural supports were wrapped in oriented strand board to mount mud-in aluminum extrusions using a pneumatic nailer. The remaining gaps were filled with additional board material, finished with drywall mud, sanded, primed, painted black, and sealed at the base with silicone caulk for spill resistance. Power injection wiring was concealed inside the corner moldings to mitigate voltage drop over the vertical spans, while thin metal tubing protected three-conductor 18 AWG wiring at the bottom of each column to reliably bridge power and data without exposing cables to the crowd.

The technical core of the installation relies on a modular, serviceable power and data distribution architecture engineered to support ten pillars, each featuring eight four-meter pixel strips across its corners and faces. Dedicated switched electrical outlets were professionally installed to provide isolated power across the system. At the top of each pillar, the individual strips converge into four consolidated data runs using a screw terminal block that interfaces with a 24-pin ATX power coupler. This coupler connects directly to a custom power distribution, fuse, and data control board housed safely above the video ceiling, ensuring safe current delivery, clean data transmission, and streamlined maintenance during live event operations.

title: Blackout Ceiling Tubes
description: Que Bueno Suerte! | Denver - 18 fanless power supplies drive a blackout 3000K pixel array below a low mezzanine HVAC duct.
longDescription:
A central HVAC duct and a low ceiling above the Que Bueno Suerte! mezzanine had already killed one designer's lighting concept years earlier. I took the lowest point of that duct as a hard clearance limit and shot a laser level across the room to hang a flat array of blackout tubes. The venue needed warm 3000K white for early evening dinner service and high-impact RGBW pixel chases for Latin dance nights. Standard milky white LED diffusion looks cheap when powered off, so I used black diffusion against the dark ceiling paint so the rig would visually disappear during the day.

I spent a month working overhead from 6ft ladders and restaurant benches, cutting strutchannel and setting cable anchors every 12 in along the beams. I originally ran 18/2 wire inside the tubes for power injection at the far end, but the wire drooped inside the casing and cast obvious shadows. I ripped the extra wiring out entirely and tested the strips from a single end, which ran full white with zero color shift.

Silent operation meant no fanned power supplies. I specced 18 waterproof MEAN WELL HLG units across 3 new 20A circuits, with each circuit powering a bank of 6 supplies and each supply driving 2 bars through independent fuses. Booting 6 fanless supplies at once tripped the breakers instantly from inrush current. I built custom sequencer boxes to stagger startup by 5 seconds so the capacitors could charge. Long-range decoders fed over 24 universes of sACN pixel data from a rack server in the office, running ENTTEC ELM before I moved the venue to Madrix 5.

The owner finally got his mezzanine installation without a low-hanging mess above the tables. The array blends into the ceiling paint by afternoon, gives a warm incandescent glow over dinner, and hits hard when the dance floor opens.
